Measurements and Units.intro: Physics describes nature with measurable quantities. A measurement is a number together with a unit; the unit gives the number meaning.

blocks.x: The seven SI base quantities are length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol) and luminous intensity (cd). Derived units come from these: velocity m s⁻¹, force newton (N = kg m s⁻²), energy joule (J = N m), pressure pascal (Pa = N m⁻²). Use prefixes such as milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶, kilo = 10³ and mega = 10⁶. Vernier calipers measure internal/external dimensions; a micrometer measures small thicknesses; a stopwatch measures time.
Convert to SI before substituting. For example, 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000/3600 = 20 m s⁻¹. Dimensions can test whether an equation is plausible, but do not prove it is physically correct.

Scalars and Vectors.intro: Some quantities are fully described by size alone; others also require direction. This distinction changes how quantities are added.

blocks.x: A scalar has magnitude only: mass, time, distance, speed, energy and temperature. A vector has magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum and electric field. Add vectors by drawing them head-to-tail or resolving them into perpendicular components. For a vector A at angle θ to the horizontal, Ax = A cos θ and Ay = A sin θ. The resultant of perpendicular components is √(Ax² + Ay²), with direction tan⁻¹(Ay/Ax).
A displacement of 3 m east followed by 4 m north gives resultant √(3² + 4²) = 5 m, at tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53.1° north of east. Distance travelled is 7 m; displacement is 5 m in a direction.

Motion.intro: Motion is a change of position with time relative to a chosen reference point. The equations of uniformly accelerated motion apply only when acceleration is constant.

blocks.x: Distance is total path length; displacement is directed change in position. Average speed = total distance/time; average velocity = displacement/time. Acceleration a = (v − u)/t. For constant a: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t. On a displacement-time graph, gradient is velocity. On a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and signed area is displacement. Free fall near Earth has g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² downward (often 10 m s⁻² in exam estimates).
A car accelerates uniformly from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. a = (25−5)/4 = 5 m s⁻²; distance = average velocity × time = ½(5+25)×4 = 60 m.

Gravitational Field.intro: Gravity is the attractive interaction between masses. A gravitational field describes the force that a mass would experience at each point.

blocks.x: Field strength g = F/m and near Earth is approximately 9.8 N kg⁻¹, equivalent to 9.8 m s⁻². Weight W = mg; mass is the amount of matter and is measured in kg, while weight is a force in N and changes with g. Newton’s universal law is F = Gm₁m₂/r². Gravitational potential energy near Earth is mgh. For a circular orbit, gravity provides centripetal force; satellites farther from Earth have lower orbital speed and longer period.
A 60 kg person has weight W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N on Earth. Their mass remains 60 kg on the Moon, but weight is smaller because lunar g is smaller.

Equilibrium of Forces.intro: An object is in mechanical equilibrium when it has no linear or angular acceleration. It may be at rest or move at constant velocity.

blocks.x: For translational equilibrium, the vector sum of forces is zero: ΣFx=0 and ΣFy=0. For rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot. Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot, measured in N m. A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces separated by a distance; its moment is one force times perpendicular separation. A body's centre of gravity is the point through which its weight acts.
A 4 N force acts 0.30 m from a pivot. Its moment is 1.2 N m. A 6 N force on the other side balances it at distance 1.2/6 = 0.20 m.

Work, Energy and Power.intro: Work is energy transferred when a force causes displacement. Energy is conserved, although it can change form or spread to the surroundings.

blocks.x: For a constant force parallel to motion, W=Fs; at angle θ, W=Fs cosθ. Kinetic energy Ek=½mv²; gravitational potential energy near Earth Ep=mgh. Power P=W/t=ΔE/t and, for steady motion under a parallel force, P=Fv. Efficiency = useful output energy/input energy ×100%. The work-energy theorem states net work equals change in kinetic energy. A negative work term means the force removes mechanical energy, for example friction.
A 2 kg object moving at 3 m s⁻¹ has Ek=½×2×3²=9 J. Raising it 4 m adds Ep=2×9.8×4=78.4 J.

Simple Machines.intro: A machine changes the size or direction of a force, or the distance over which it acts. It cannot create energy.

blocks.x: Mechanical advantage MA = load/effort. Velocity ratio VR = distance moved by effort/distance moved by load. Efficiency = MA/VR ×100%. For an ideal machine, input work equals output work and MA=VR. In a lever, moments about the pivot balance; a pulley system's ideal VR equals the number of rope sections supporting the moving load. Examples include levers, pulleys, wheel-and-axle, inclined planes, screws and gears.
A machine lifts 240 N using 60 N effort. MA=4. If VR=5, efficiency=4/5×100%=80%.

Friction.intro: Friction is a contact force that opposes relative motion or its tendency between surfaces. It can be useful for walking and braking, but it dissipates mechanical energy as heat.

blocks.x: Static friction adjusts up to a limiting value; kinetic/sliding friction acts during sliding. In the simple model, limiting friction Fmax=μR, where μ is the coefficient of friction and R is the normal reaction. Friction depends on surface materials and normal force; the model often treats it as independent of apparent contact area. Lubrication, polishing, ball bearings and streamlining reduce different kinds of resistance.
If μ=0.25 and R=80 N, limiting friction is 0.25×80=20 N. A 12 N pull can be balanced by 12 N static friction; motion does not start yet.

Elasticity.intro: Elasticity is the ability of a material to regain its original shape after a deforming force is removed. Deformation beyond the elastic limit may be permanent.

blocks.x: Hooke’s law states extension is proportional to applied force while the elastic limit is not exceeded: F=kx, where k is stiffness in N m⁻¹. Stress=force/cross-sectional area (Pa); strain=extension/original length (dimensionless). Young modulus E=stress/strain. Elastic potential energy in a spring is ½kx², equal to the area under a straight-line force-extension graph.
A spring extends 0.04 m under 8 N. k=8/0.04=200 N m⁻¹. At this extension its stored energy is ½×200×0.04²=0.16 J.

Pressure.intro: Pressure measures force distributed over an area. The same force produces greater pressure on a smaller area.

A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; a manometer compares gas pressure with a reference pressure.

Liquids at Rest.intro: A liquid at rest exerts pressure on the walls and bottom of its container. Pressure grows with depth because deeper layers support more liquid above them.

blocks.x: Hydrostatic pressure p=ρgh. Upthrust is the resultant upward force from the pressure difference between the bottom and top of an immersed body. Archimedes’ principle: upthrust equals the weight of displaced fluid. An object floats when upthrust balances its weight; its average density is then less than the liquid's density. For a floating body, fraction submerged ≈ object density/liquid density. Communicating vessels settle at equal levels when exposed to the same pressure.
A 0.002 m³ object is fully immersed in water. Upthrust=ρgV=1000×9.8×0.002=19.6 N.

Temperature and Its Measurement.intro: Temperature indicates how hot or cold a body is and determines the direction of net thermal energy transfer. It is not the same as heat energy.

blocks.x: Thermometers use a thermometric property that changes reproducibly, such as liquid volume, electrical resistance or thermocouple voltage. Celsius and Kelvin scales are related by T(K)=θ(°C)+273.15. For a linear scale, θ=(X−X₀)/(X₁−X₀)×100°C between ice and steam points. Clinical thermometers have a narrow range; laboratory thermometers usually do not have a constriction. Absolute zero is 0 K (−273.15°C).
A temperature of 27°C is 300.15 K, approximately 300 K. A change of 1°C equals a change of 1 K.

Thermal Expansion.intro: Most materials expand when heated because their particles vibrate more strongly and their average separation increases. Expansion matters in bridges, railway tracks, pipes and thermometers.

blocks.x: For small temperature changes, linear expansion ΔL=αL₀ΔT; area expansion is approximately 2αA₀ΔT and volume expansion approximately 3αV₀ΔT for isotropic solids. α is the coefficient of linear expansion in K⁻¹. Liquids show apparent expansion because both liquid and container expand; anomalous expansion of water occurs between 0°C and 4°C, with maximum density at 4°C. Bimetallic strips bend because their metals have different α values.

Quantity of Heat.intro: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A body's temperature change depends on its mass, material and heat capacity.

blocks.x: For a temperature change without change of state, Q=mcΔT, where c is specific heat capacity in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Heat capacity C=Q/ΔT=mc. In calorimetry, energy lost by hotter bodies equals energy gained by cooler bodies in an insulated system. Electrical heating energy can be found from Q=VIt=I²Rt. Some energy may escape to the surroundings, so measured values can differ from ideal predictions.
Heating 0.50 kg of water by 20 K needs Q=0.50×4200×20=42,000 J.

Change of State.intro: Matter changes between solid, liquid and gas when energy changes particle arrangement and separation. During a pure substance's phase change at fixed pressure, temperature remains constant while latent heat is transferred.

blocks.x: Specific latent heat L=Q/m, so Q=mL. Latent heat of fusion changes solid to liquid; latent heat of vaporization changes liquid to gas. The heating curve has sloping sections (temperature changes; Q=mcΔT) and flat sections (state changes; Q=mL). Melting and freezing, boiling and condensation are reverse processes. Evaporation occurs at the surface below boiling point and causes cooling; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point.
Melting 0.20 kg of ice at 0°C requires Q=mLf=0.20×3.34×10⁵=6.68×10⁴ J.

Vapours.intro: A vapour is the gaseous form of a substance that is normally liquid or solid under the stated conditions. Evaporation and condensation establish vapour pressure in a closed space.

blocks.x: Saturated vapour is in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature; its pressure is the saturated vapour pressure. Vapour pressure rises with temperature. Relative humidity = actual water-vapour pressure/saturated vapour pressure at that temperature ×100%. Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated as it cools. Evaporation is faster with greater exposed area, higher temperature, moving air and lower humidity. Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals external pressure.
If actual vapour pressure is 1.2 kPa and saturation pressure is 2.0 kPa, relative humidity=60%.
